{
  "analyses": [
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-3758-s13423-026-02985-6",
      "title": "Let it go: How trusted reminders alter intention maintenance",
      "research_question": "Does experience with reminders of different perceived reliability cause people to shift from internally maintaining prospective intentions to relying on external reminders?",
      "methodology": "The authors ran a two-session prospective-memory experiment with 320 university students using a 2 × 3 × 2 mixed design crossing session, reminder reliability (0%, 50%, or 100%), and reminder availability at retrieval. Participants encoded prospective-memory word pairs while performing a lexical-decision task, and intermittent thought probes during the retention interval measured whether they were thinking about the prospective-memory task, the ongoing task, or unrelated material. Session 1 established experience with reminder support, while Session 2 manipulated expected reliability and unexpectedly withheld reminders from some participants. Three-way ANOVAs and corrected post-hoc tests were reported with effect sizes, confidence intervals, and Bayes factors.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "During the initial trust session, reminders improved prospective-memory performance without reducing prospective-memory-related thoughts, which is consistent with duplicative rather than immediately substitutive offloading.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results; General discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "After experience with reliable support, participants expecting 100% reliable reminders reported substantially fewer prospective-memory-related thoughts than both the no-reminder and 50%-reliability groups.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results — Prospective memory (PM)-related thoughts"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The 100%-reliability condition also produced more ongoing-task-related thoughts, while reminder reliability did not meaningfully alter task-unrelated thought.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results — Task-related thoughts; Task-unrelated thoughts"
        },
        {
          "finding": "When reminders remained available in Session 2, both reminder groups substantially outperformed the no-reminder group in prospective-memory accuracy.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results — PM accuracy"
        },
        {
          "finding": "When expected reminders were unexpectedly absent, the 100%-reliability group performed worse than the no-reminder group, but the associated Bayes factor was equivocal, so the authors characterize this result as suggestive rather than definitive.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results — PM accuracy"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Participants in the 50%-reliability condition continued to maintain prospective-memory-related thought, and their unaided performance did not fall below the no-reminder condition when reminders were withdrawn.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results; General discussion"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The retention intervals were brief and reminders were imposed by the experimenter, limiting ecological validity for long-lived real-world intentions.",
        "Thought-probe categories were mutually exclusive, so increases in one category necessarily redistribute responses away from other categories.",
        "The participants were university undergraduates rather than workers managing naturally occurring obligations.",
        "The experiment examines individual prospective intentions rather than longitudinal cross-thread work-item states such as new, open, resolved, or superseded items.",
        "It does not evaluate obligation-versus-preference selection or joint omission, repetition, and false-alert outcomes.",
        "Forty-nine participants received invalid response options on one post-experimental verification question, although most had independently demonstrated target detection."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "initial_duplicative_offloading": 0.98,
        "trusted_reminders_reduce_intention_thought": 0.99,
        "attention_redistribution_to_ongoing_task": 0.98,
        "reminders_improve_supported_retrieval": 0.99,
        "withdrawal_cost_after_full_reliability": 0.82,
        "uncertainty_preserves_internal_maintenance": 0.94
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The final analyzed sample contained 320 participants.",
        "The design manipulated reminder reliability at 0%, 50%, and 100%.",
        "Thought probes were collected before retrieval and served as a real-time measure of conscious intention maintenance.",
        "Reminder groups showed enhanced prospective-memory performance during the initial trust session without fewer prospective-memory thoughts.",
        "In the critical session, the 100%-reliability group reported fewer prospective-memory-related thoughts than the other reliability groups.",
        "The 100%-reliability group reported more ongoing-task-related thoughts in the critical session.",
        "Task-unrelated thought did not show meaningful pairwise differences across reminder-reliability conditions.",
        "Unexpected withdrawal of a fully trusted reminder produced a small, statistically significant but Bayes-factor-equivocal accuracy decrement relative to no reminders.",
        "Data, materials, and analysis scripts are provided through the Open Science Framework."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-026-02985-6",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-18653-v1-2020-acl-main-122",
      "title": "Examining the State-of-the-Art in News Timeline Summarization",
      "research_question": "Which high-level strategies for news timeline summarization perform best under end-to-end temporal evaluation, and what dataset characteristics make longitudinal timeline construction difficult?",
      "methodology": "The paper compares direct summarization, a date-wise strategy, and event-clustering approaches to timeline summarization, with the proposed date-wise method exploiting publication dates and textual temporal expressions to identify candidate dates before summarizing each selected date. Temporal expressions are extracted and sentence selection is performed using date-related representations, while the clustering alternative uses temporally constrained document clustering. Evaluation covers the T17, Crisis, and newly introduced Entities datasets, the latter containing 47 topics and averaging 4,437 days of coverage per topic. Systems are evaluated with alignment-based ROUGE F1 and Date-F1 using leave-one-out cross-validation over tasks and approximate-randomization significance tests.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The Datewise system achieved the highest alignment-based ROUGE results among evaluated non-oracle methods on all three benchmark datasets.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.4 Results; 6.1 Performance of TLS Strategies"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Datewise did not consistently dominate in Date-F1, indicating that much of its advantage came from sentence selection and summarization rather than superior date prediction alone.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.1 Performance of TLS Strategies"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The new Entities benchmark substantially extends longitudinal coverage, with 47 topics, 47 timelines, an average of 959 documents and 600 publication dates per task, and an average duration of about 12 years.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4 Dataset"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The clustering approach generally underperformed Datewise and the prior Martschat method, with analysis showing that nearby articles were sometimes merged even when ground-truth timelines treated them as separate events.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.1 Performance of TLS Strategies"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Automatically generated timelines frequently contained adjacent-date redundancy, and simply prohibiting adjacent dates reduced the automatic evaluation scores, exposing a mismatch between redundancy control and the evaluated objectives.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.4 Adjacent Dates and Redundancy"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Datewise and the clustering method were substantially faster than the combinatorial prior system, and the prior system could not be run on Crisis because of memory requirements.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.3 Running Time; Appendix A.4"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Even the improved systems remained far from oracle performance, leaving substantial room for better longitudinal event selection and summarization.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7 Conclusion"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Human editorial decisions about which events belong in a timeline and how they should be summarized are subjective.",
        "The available article collections may omit important events, so system evaluation can be constrained by source coverage rather than summarization quality alone.",
        "The Entities input collection was retrieved from a single news provider, The Guardian.",
        "Article headlines were excluded from the main experiments partly to preserve comparability with earlier work and because T17 lacks titles.",
        "Adjacent-date redundancy remains unresolved, and automatic metrics can reward redundancy rather than a balanced temporal spread.",
        "The work models news events rather than workplace obligations and does not track explicit new, open, resolved, or superseded work-item states.",
        "It does not model obligation-versus-preference selection, adaptive personalization, preference drift, or joint omission/repetition/false-alert evaluation."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "datewise_best_alignment_scores": 0.99,
        "date_selection_not_sole_advantage": 0.98,
        "entities_long_horizon_benchmark": 0.99,
        "clustering_granularity_problem": 0.96,
        "redundancy_metric_mismatch": 0.98,
        "scalability_advantage": 0.99,
        "large_oracle_gap": 0.98
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The study evaluates timeline summarization end to end rather than considering only date selection or date summarization in isolation.",
        "The Entities dataset contains 47 topics and 47 ground-truth timelines.",
        "Entities averages 959 documents, 31,545 sentences, and 600 publication dates per task.",
        "The average Entities task spans 4,437 days, or approximately 12 years.",
        "Datewise has the strongest alignment-based ROUGE performance across T17, Crisis, and Entities.",
        "Date-F1 is not always better for Datewise than for competing methods.",
        "Large numbers of articles and publication dates generally make timeline tasks harder.",
        "Adjacent dates often produce repeated descriptions of the same event.",
        "The authors recommend treating automatic timeline metrics cautiously and supplementing them with qualitative analysis or user studies.",
        "The paper provides the Entities dataset through the news-tls repository."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2005.10107",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2609.02465",
      "title": "Can Risk-Based Alerting Mitigate Cybersecurity Alert Fatigue?",
      "research_question": "Can combinations of interpretable risk-based alerting hypotheses reliably prioritize true cybersecurity alerts over false alerts across heterogeneous environments strongly enough to reduce analyst workload?",
      "methodology": "The authors formulate risk-based alerting as continuous prioritization and implement five risk modules—Rule Level, Accumulation, Variety, Rarity, and Aperiodicity—in the CATS experimentation framework. They evaluate these modules and weighted combinations on eight alert datasets covering Falco, Sigma, Suricata, and Wazuh data from one enterprise environment and four testbeds. AUROC is the primary metric, with parameter studies and leave-one-dataset-out weight selection used to examine robustness on unseen datasets. Additional evaluation uses average precision, an inverse balanced Brier-score measure of calibration, type-adjusted variants, and a composite skill score.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The optimized leave-one-out weighted pipeline achieved mean AUROC 0.92 with standard deviation 0.09 across eight datasets, compared with 0.72 and standard deviation 0.21 for straightforward rule-severity prioritization.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7.2 Combining Modules Works Even Better"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Rule Level, Accumulation, and Variety each distinguished true from false alerts significantly above chance across datasets, whereas Rarity and Aperiodicity did not show significant above-chance aggregate performance.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "8 Discussion and Limitations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Weights obtained from the other datasets generalized well in leave-one-out evaluation, suggesting that the combined prioritization strategy was relatively robust to changes in environment, alert source, and attack.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7.2 Combining Modules Works Even Better"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The broader multi-metric evaluation was mostly above corresponding no-skill levels, although individual datasets exposed weaknesses that AUROC alone did not capture.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7.3 Digging Deeper with Multiple Metrics"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Using trailing rather than centered temporal windows reduced mean AUROC for the reference pipeline by about 17%, exposing a trade-off between immediate alerting and using future neighboring alerts for stronger prioritization.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7.2; 8 Discussion and Limitations"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The study does not directly establish a reduction in human alert fatigue because analysts were not experimentally studied; the fatigue benefit is inferred from reduced false-alert workload and the authors call for SOC-analyst user studies.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "8 Discussion and Limitations"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Only the ERPCorp Falco dataset contains benign activity captured from a real corporate network; the other evaluated environments rely on testbeds and simulated users.",
        "Some SOCBED- and APT29S2-based datasets are short, which limits conclusions for long temporal windows.",
        "The real enterprise ERPCorp dataset cannot be published because of security and privacy restrictions.",
        "Centered windows improve some prioritization results but necessarily delay prioritization until future alerts within half of the window are available.",
        "Human alert fatigue, analyst trust, usability, and behavioral response to prioritization were not directly measured.",
        "The study evaluates security alerts rather than cross-thread workplace briefing or explicit work-item lifecycle states.",
        "It does not jointly evaluate briefing-style omissions, repetitions, and false alerts."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "combined_pipeline_auroc": 0.99,
        "three_effective_risk_modules": 0.99,
        "leave_one_out_robustness": 0.98,
        "multi_metric_support": 0.96,
        "temporal_window_latency_tradeoff": 0.99,
        "human_fatigue_not_directly_tested": 1.0
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The evaluation contains eight alert datasets drawn from five environments.",
        "Five independently parameterized risk hypotheses are implemented as alert-scoring modules.",
        "The leave-one-out combined pipeline reaches a mean AUROC of 0.92 across the datasets.",
        "Straightforward rule-level prioritization has a mean AUROC of 0.72.",
        "Rule Level, Accumulation, and Variety perform significantly above chance in the aggregate tests.",
        "Rarity and Aperiodicity do not show significant aggregate improvement over chance.",
        "Average precision and a balanced Brier-derived calibration metric complement AUROC in the practical evaluation.",
        "Centered temporal windows provide better performance for some modules but prevent instantaneous prioritization.",
        "Most evaluated datasets are testbed based rather than recordings of normal corporate activity.",
        "Future user studies with SOC analysts are needed to measure alert-fatigue effects directly.",
        "CATS code and most evaluated datasets are publicly provided, while the corporate ERPCorp dataset is withheld."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.02465",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-2196-43977",
      "title": "Effect of Personalized Email-Based Reminders on Participants’ Timeliness in an Online Education Program: Randomized Controlled Trial",
      "research_question": "Do progress-personalized email reminders improve the timeliness of adult online learners more than general schedule-based reminders?",
      "methodology": "Thirty-nine professional learners from Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Kenya participating in the OneLearns online program were randomized into an AB-BA reminder design over the course. All participants received weekly email reminders, but personalized reminders additionally reported the participant's observed progress while general reminders only described where the participant should be according to the schedule. Across five months the study sent 585 reminders, comprising 390 general and 195 personalized reminders. A Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression estimated the probability of being on time while accounting for participant and reminder-time variation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The model-estimated probability of being on time was 14 percentage points higher after personalized reminders than after general reminders, with a 95% credible interval from 3 to 25 percentage points.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "In the unadjusted observations, 64.1% of personalized reminders were followed by an on-time state compared with 52.8% of general reminders.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results — Reminder Data"
        },
        {
          "finding": "For an average participant at an average reminder time, the model estimated a 70% probability of being on time after personalized reminders and 56% after general reminders.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Results — Reminder Data"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A relatively small amount of state-specific personalization—telling a learner both expected and observed progress—was sufficient to improve timeliness relative to schedule-only reminders in this sample.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Discussion — Principal Findings"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The study had no no-reminder arm, so it estimates the incremental value of personalization over general reminders rather than the causal effect of reminders versus receiving no reminder.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Study Design"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Personalized reminders improved the procrastination problem but did not eliminate it.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Conclusions"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The sample contains only 39 participants, limiting precision and generalizability.",
        "Participants were adult professionals from three East African countries in one specialized online education program.",
        "There was no untreated no-reminder control condition.",
        "The intervention personalizes reminders from current progress but does not learn changing individual reminder preferences.",
        "The study does not evaluate preference drift, obligation-versus-preference selection, or cross-thread work-item state transitions.",
        "It measures timeliness rather than a joint set of omission, repetition, and false-alert outcomes.",
        "The underlying participant data are available only by request from the institution rather than through an unrestricted public download."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "personalization_improves_timeliness": 0.99,
        "raw_timeliness_difference": 0.99,
        "model_probabilities": 0.99,
        "small_progress_personalization_effective": 0.96,
        "no_no_reminder_comparison": 1.0,
        "procrastination_not_eliminated": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The study enrolled 39 active professional learners.",
        "Participants came from Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Kenya.",
        "The intervention sent 585 weekly email reminders over five months.",
        "Personalized reminders included both where the learner should be and the learner's observed current progress.",
        "General reminders described the expected course pace without reporting the learner's observed progress.",
        "Personalized reminders were followed by on-time status in 64.1% of observations, compared with 52.8% after general reminders.",
        "The Bayesian model estimated a 14-percentage-point advantage for personalized reminders.",
        "The 95% credible interval for the estimated advantage was 3 to 25 percentage points.",
        "Personalization improved timeliness but did not eliminate procrastination.",
        "The article supplies a Python program used to convert progress percentages into page numbers.",
        "The study data can be requested from KTH's Registrar's Office."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://formative.jmir.org/2023/1/e43977",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2403.19795",
      "title": "Learning Human Preferences Over Robot Behavior as Soft Planning Constraints",
      "research_question": "Can preferences over robot behavior be represented as soft planning constraints and inferred from noisy pairwise trajectory choices while keeping task requirements as hard constraints?",
      "methodology": "The study represents user preferences as soft PDDL planning constraints while retaining task objectives as hard constraints, and evaluates the formulation in Habitat 2.0 rearrangement tasks using the OPTIC planner. Simulated users answer binary comparisons between possible robot trajectories under a bounded-rationality choice model with several noise levels. Neural preference predictors based on sequence representations are trained with either single-target, preference-distribution, or noisy-distribution supervision on a generated dataset of 2,627,664 examples split 60/20/20 into training, validation, and test sets. Models receive ten preference queries and are evaluated with True Positive Rate (TPR) and Accepted Output Rate (AOR).",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The framework explicitly separates mandatory task goals from nonmandatory behavioral preferences by representing the latter as soft PDDL constraints with costs.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "III Problem Formulation; VII Conclusion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The learned models could infer the three simulated preference types under noisy user choices, although increasing choice noise reduced absolute prediction performance.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V Results; VI Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "When both training and evaluation were noise-free, the learned approach underperformed the perfectly rational baseline, whereas models trained and tested with noisy choices performed similarly to or better than that baseline at the corresponding noise levels.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V Results — RQ1"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Training with a small amount of choice noise generalized better to noisy evaluation data than training without noise, while increasing training noise further did not produce additional gains.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V Results — RQ2"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Distribution-based supervision was often similar to or better than single-target supervision under low or no training noise, but this advantage was not universal at higher noise levels.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V Results — RQ3"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The experiments assume that a user's preferences and the task objective remain constant over time, so adaptive preference learning under preference drift is not evaluated.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "III Problem Formulation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "All evaluated user choices were simulated rather than collected from real people, and real-time adaptation with human users is left for future work.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "IV Evaluation Setup; VI-A Limitations & Future Work"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The paper explicitly assumes that human preferences and task objectives do not change over time.",
        "Only a small subset of preferences expressible in PDDL is evaluated.",
        "Preference queries are predefined rather than selected adaptively according to current uncertainty.",
        "The experiments use simulated bounded-rational user choices instead of feedback from real people.",
        "Evaluation centers on a simulated household rearrangement setting rather than workplace communication.",
        "The study does not track longitudinal cross-thread work-item states or evaluate omission, repetition, and false-alert briefing errors.",
        "No public code or generated dataset release is identified in the paper."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": false,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "soft_vs_hard_constraint_formulation": 0.99,
        "preference_inference_under_noise": 0.97,
        "noise_relative_to_rational_baseline": 0.98,
        "small_training_noise_improves_generalization": 0.99,
        "supervision_effect_depends_on_noise": 0.98,
        "preferences_assumed_stationary": 1.0,
        "no_real_user_evaluation": 1.0
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The approach expresses desired but nonmandatory robot behavior as soft planning constraints.",
        "The evaluation considers three kinds of simulated human preference.",
        "User choices are generated with a bounded-rationality model at multiple noise levels.",
        "The generated dataset contains 2,627,664 examples.",
        "Training, validation, and test partitions use a 60/20/20 split without repeating trajectory pairs and preferences across partitions.",
        "TPR requires every component of a predicted preference to be correct.",
        "AOR measures whether a predicted preference is consistent with the supplied non-noisy queries.",
        "Performance declines as simulated user choices become noisier.",
        "Training on a small amount of noise improves generalization to other noisy conditions relative to noise-free training.",
        "The formulation assumes preferences do not change over time or because of interaction.",
        "The authors identify adaptive query selection and real-world human evaluation as future work."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2403.19795",
      "access": "full_text"
    }
  ],
  "skipped": []
}
